claims.text: Introducing a controlled amount of a Ni-based interlayer or Ni dopant during sintering can enable transient liquid-phase sintering in a W–Cu composite.
The Ni addition will produce an in situ graded interface in the W–Cu composite.
The graded interlayer will contain Ni-rich phases that wet both W and Cu.
The Ni-rich graded interlayer will bridge the W–Cu interface and minimize void-nucleation sites.
The Ni-based interlayer lowers the interfacial energy between W and Cu during sintering.
Lower interfacial energy promotes a transient liquid phase that facilitates interdiffusion.
Ni-assisted processing promotes metastable interfacial compounds that form a continuous bond.
The continuous interfacial bond mitigates phase separation under subsequent thermal and irradiation stresses.
The continuous interfacial bond suppresses interfacial void formation under subsequent thermal and irradiation stresses.
Ni-modified W–Cu will have higher effective thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Ni-modified W–Cu will retain a more stable and void-free interfacial microstructure than untreated W–Cu under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu is susceptible to phase separation and interfacial void formation during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Phase separation and interfacial void formation in untreated W–Cu reduce its thermal conductivity.
The intervention is applicable only below temperatures at which Ni diffuses excessively or forms deleterious intermetallic compounds.
The intervention should remain effective at irradiation doses typical of current plasma-facing and cooling applications.
The optimal Ni concentration for interface grading without unwanted intermetallic formation is unknown.
The long-term irradiation stability of the Ni-modified W–Cu interface has not been established.
